items.stem: A Massachusetts resident pharmacy learns on Friday that an incorrect-strength prescription it dispensed caused a patient serious injury. A CQI investigation is already open. What additional Board duty applies?

choices.text: Send only a quarterly CQI summary to the Board.
choices.why: A serious-injury improper dispensing event triggers independent, timely reporting.

choices.text: Report only if the injured patient files a malpractice lawsuit.
choices.why: 247 CMR 20.02 does not make a civil claim a prerequisite.

choices.text: Wait for a court to determine negligence before reporting.
choices.why: The duty is tied to discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing, not a final liability judgment.

choices.text: The Manager of Record must report the improper dispensing to the Board within seven business days of discovery.
choices.why: 247 CMR 20.02(1) imposes this separate Board-reporting duty.

items.stem: A Massachusetts resident pharmacy compounds a preparation, and an employee learns of a serious adverse drug event from a patient's use of the pharmacy-compounded product. Which recipients are required under 247 CMR 20.02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy.
choices.why: The regulation expressly names the Board.

choices.text: FDA MedWatch Program.
choices.why: The federal adverse-event program is specifically listed in the state reporting rule.

choices.text: Only the patient's employer, instead of any public authority.
choices.why: An employer notification is not a substitute for the named mandatory reports.

choices.text: Betsy Lehman Center for Patient Safety and Medical Error Reduction.
choices.why: The Massachusetts reporting provision names this center as an additional recipient.

items.stem: A pharmacist Manager of Record submitted a report to the Massachusetts Board about improper dispensing that caused death. Staff propose deleting the associated incident records three years after filing because the CQI program is complete. What is the minimum retention under the specific reporting rule?

choices.text: Only until the next monthly CQI meeting.
choices.why: Reporting records carry a separate minimum retention period.

choices.text: At least five years after the Board report was filed, with records readily retrievable.
choices.why: 247 CMR 20.02(4) expressly requires a minimum five years from report filing.

choices.text: Exactly two years from the original prescription date.
choices.why: The two-year rule is not the specific five-year serious-event reporting retention.

choices.text: No retention requirement exists once the Board acknowledges receipt.
choices.why: Acknowledgment does not remove the stated five-year duty.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is arrested on November 6, 2026. The pharmacist reports it promptly to their pharmacy employer, but the employer does not relay it to the Board. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The individual licensee remains responsible for reporting the arrest to the Board within 14 calendar days.
choices.why: 247 CMR 20.03(3) makes this an individual licensee duty; internal employer notification alone is insufficient.

choices.text: The duty starts only after conviction.
choices.why: The rule separately lists arrests and pending criminal charges.

choices.text: Employer notice is enough because an individual has no Board reporting duty.
choices.why: The requirement is on each individual Board licensee.

choices.text: An arrest report must wait for the next pharmacist license renewal.
choices.why: The rule sets a 14-calendar-day period.

items.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy proposes keeping its Schedule II morphine stock in an unlocked automated room because the system has a digital audit trail. Under DPH hospital accountability guidelines, which control remains necessary?

choices.text: A digital log eliminates the need to secure bulk Schedule II stock.
choices.why: An electronic audit trail does not replace physical access controls.

choices.text: Any licensed hospital employee may access bulk Schedule II stock without pharmacist oversight.
choices.why: Hospital pharmacy vault access is restricted to licensed pharmacists under the guideline.

choices.text: A vault or equivalent security with pharmacist-restricted access and a hard-copy perpetual inventory.
choices.why: The DPH hospital/clinic guideline specifically addresses physical Schedule II security and hard-copy perpetual accountability.

choices.text: Periodic refill counts alone replace Schedule II perpetual tracking.
choices.why: The guideline requires perpetual accounting for these drugs.

choices.text: Allow mixing because Schedule III–IV medicines may be stored like Schedule VI in this setting.

choices.why: This applies the hospital-specific noncommingling, access and inventory requirements.

items.stem: A Massachusetts hospital nursing unit uses an electronic controlled cabinet for Schedule II–V medications. Which operational requirements are described by DPH's general accountability guideline? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Keep Schedule II–V medication in double-locked, permanently affixed storage with perpetual inventory.
choices.why: The guideline expressly specifies this for nursing units.

choices.text: Conduct and document a QA review of administered controlled substances at least weekly.
choices.why: The nursing-unit general section requires no less than weekly QA review.

choices.text: Limit access to authorized licensed staff and use tamper-resistant packaging.
choices.why: Both restrictions are stated in the nursing-unit requirements.

choices.text: Skip controlled waste documentation whenever an electronic cabinet tracks door openings.
choices.why: Door access logs do not replace accountability for administration and wasting.

items.stem: A hospital nurse gives part of an ordered Schedule II injection and must discard the unused remainder. Two licensed staff are available; a supervisor suggests that a single unlicensed orderly may document the waste. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Use two licensed staff to conduct and co-sign the disposal and document the administered and wasted amounts.
choices.why: The DPH guideline specifies two licensed staff and appropriate signed documentation for unused Schedule II–V portions.

choices.text: Have the orderly alone discard it as ordinary trash.
choices.why: An unlicensed orderly cannot substitute for the designated licensed witness/waste process.

choices.text: Enter the unused remainder as an intact, never-administered pharmacy return.
choices.why: A partial dose remaining after patient administration is not an intact returned unit.

choices.text: Wait for a pharmacy technician to remove the cabinet from service indefinitely.
choices.why: The guideline provides a documented, witnessed wasting route rather than an indefinite hold.

items.stem: The Massachusetts pharmacy's Manager of Record knows they will be away for 45 days starting next month. The owner plans to appoint an interim manager only on day 20 of the absence. What is required instead?

choices.text: An interim manager is never necessary if the MOR remains licensed.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.23 addresses extended absences regardless of continued licensure.

choices.text: Appoint a Board-registered interim manager before the planned absence, with the required controlled-substance inventory.
choices.why: A planned absence expected to last 30 days or more triggers prior appointment and an inventory.

choices.text: Simply put the name of the busiest technician on the duty roster.
choices.why: An interim MOR must be a registered pharmacist and meet Board requirements.

choices.text: Wait until the absence passes 100 days.
choices.why: The 100-day threshold relates to a change-of-MOR application, not the 30-day interim trigger.
